intro: Rachmaninoff recorded his Prelude in C♯ minor, Op. 3 No. 2, in New York in April 1928, thirty-six years after he wrote it. The quiet chords of the opening return later, spread across the whole keyboard.

sections.label: A · Lento, three low notes, then triplets
sections.mNote: Three low notes open the Lento.

sections.label: B · Agitato in triplets
sections.mNote: The Agitato melody rises above running triplets.

sections.label: C · Descending chords, return of opening
sections.mNote: The fast passage leads back to the opening chords.

sections.label: D · Slow chords over held C♯
sections.mNote: A held bass supports the last slow chords.

cues.title: Opening, bars 1–4
cues.text: Three low notes, A–G♯–C♯, sound in octaves. Rachmaninoff marks them fortissimo. The chords that follow are marked ppp.
cues.evidence: Bosworth (1896) and Universal Edition (1910), opening upbeat and bars 1–4; Petro Kostandy’s Mutopia engraving. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Agitato, divided right hand
cues.text: In the Agitato (bars 14–21), the right hand plays a descending E–D♯–D♮–C♯ melody above triplet quavers. The left hand takes low bass notes, then moves up into a separate line in reply to the melody.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 14–21: separately stemmed upper melody, triplet quavers and the answering left-hand line. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Recording sessions, 1928
cues.text: On 21 March 1928 Rachmaninoff made three takes of the Prelude in Camden, New Jersey, and Victor discarded all three. He recorded it again in New York on 4 April. The second take from that day became the published record.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor matrix BVE-25650: takes 19–21 marked Destroy; takes 22–23 dated 4 April 1928, with take 23 the master. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/700010910/BVE-25650-Prelude_in_C_sharp_minor

cues.title: Return of the opening, four staves
cues.text: At Tempo primo the opening returns, greatly enlarged. The score sets the piano on four staves and marks the chords fff pesante. The bass continues its repeated notes while both hands play the tune in octaves.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 45–48: four-stave notation, Tempo primo and fff pesante. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Final bars over C♯ pedal
cues.text: The closing chords sound over a low C♯ held across the bars. The last chord is C♯ minor, ppp, with a fermata above it.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 55–61: C♯ pedal and final ppp chord with fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
